The harp lute is a chordophone combining features of the harp and the lute, Hornbostel–Sachs number 323-5, also called the dital harp. Its pear-shaped body joins a curved neck, supported by a pillar or by an arm projecting from the body, and it has twelve gut strings. The curved fretboard runs almost parallel to the neck and is fitted with frets; each string also has a thumb key, and pressing it brings a stopping ring down on the string against the fret, shortening the sounding length and raising the pitch by a semitone, while the other strings are stopped much as on a lute. Edward Light invented the instrument in 1795, and an earlier form appears in Bosch's Garden of Earthly Delights of about 1500.

It was invented in 1795 by Edward Light, and an earlier form appears in a painting by Hieronymus Bosch of about 1500. Its other name, dital harp, stresses that the keys are worked by the thumb, unlike the harp's pedals. In 1816 an improved version, the British harp lute, was patented. Related attempts include the lyra-guitarre of early nineteenth-century Germany, the accord-guitarre of the mid nineteenth century, and the keyed guitar.
